title: Chapter 76 — The Battering-Ram
paragraphs: Before leaving the Sperm Whale's head for now, I would have you, as a sensible observer of nature, simply and particularly examine its front, in all its compacted density. I would have you investigate it with the sole aim of forming for yourself some honest, intelligent estimate of whatever destructive power that front might be capable of.

You observe that in the ordinary swimming position of the Sperm Whale, the front of his head presents an almost entirely vertical surface to the water. You observe that the lower part of that front slopes considerably backward, providing more of a retreat for the long socket that receives the boom-like lower jaw. You observe that the mouth is entirely under the head, much like a fireplace beneath a massive mantelpiece. You further observe that this front of the head has no nose, eyes, ears, or mouth — nothing but a broad blankness of forehead, pleated with riddles. You observe also that the front of his head is almost all solid bone, covered only by a thin layer of skin and muscle. Now, mark this: below the outer layer of the skull lies a solid mass of the most wonderfully dense material. And between that mass and the huge vertical bone of the skull, which is very thick itself, lies another mass of tremendous density. These two masses together form the Sperm Whale's battering-ram.

Think of another thing. When two large, loaded ships chance to crowd and crush toward each other in the docks, what do the sailors do? They do not suspend between them, at the point of contact, any merely hard substance like iron or wood. No, they hold there a large round wad of tow and cork, enclosed in the thickest and toughest of ox-hide. That absorbs the blow. And so, in the Sperm Whale, a kind of padding exists between the solid bone of the skull and the solid mass of the case above. This wadding is not simply fat or blubber. It is something much tougher and more elastic.

Now, mark. Unerringly driving this dead, impregnable, uninjurable wall, with this most buoyant thing within — there swims behind it all a mass of tremendous life, only to be adequately measured as piled wood is measured — by the cord. And all obedient to one will, as the smallest insect. So that when I speak of the Sperm Whale's battering-ram, I am not speaking of some dull mindless force. I am speaking of a directed, calculating intelligence backed by the most tremendous physical power in the animal kingdom. What object, no matter how strong, could withstand such a battering?
